title: Act 1, Scene 2 — A Camp near Forres
paragraphs: [Alarum within. Enter King Duncan, Malcolm, Donalbain, Lennox, with Attendants, meeting a bleeding Captain.]
DUNCAN. Who is that bloody man? By the look of him, he can give us the latest news of the revolt.
MALCOLM. This is the sergeant who fought like a good, hardy soldier to keep me from being captured.—Hail, brave friend! Tell the King what you know of the fight, as you left it.

SOLDIER. It hung in the balance—like two exhausted swimmers clinging together and smothering each other's strokes. The merciless Macdonwald—well fit to be a rebel, since every kind of villainy nature can breed swarms upon him—was reinforced from the Western Isles with light-armed foot soldiers and heavy-armed fighters; and Fortune, smiling on his cursed cause, seemed for a while to play the rebel's whore. But none of it was enough. Brave Macbeth—he well deserves that name—scorning Fortune, sword drawn and smoking with bloody slaughter, cut his way through like Valor's favorite, until he faced the traitor; and, sparing him neither handshake nor farewell, he ripped him open from navel to jaw and set his head upon our battlements.
DUNCAN. Oh, valiant cousin! Worthy gentleman!

SOLDIER. Just as ship-wrecking storms and fearsome thunder break from the point where the sun begins to shine, so from that very spring where comfort seemed to rise, discomfort now wells up. Mark this, King of Scotland, mark it: no sooner had justice, armed with valor, forced these fleeing foot soldiers to trust their heels, than the Norwegian lord, seeing his chance, renewed the attack with polished weapons and fresh troops.
DUNCAN. Did this not dismay our captains, Macbeth and Banquo?

SOLDIER. Yes—as sparrows dismay eagles, or the hare the lion. To tell the truth, I must report they stood like cannons overloaded with a double charge: so they struck the enemy twice as hard, redoubling every blow. Whether they meant to bathe in steaming wounds or make the field a second Golgotha, I cannot say—but I grow faint; my wounds cry out for help.
DUNCAN. Your words become you as well as your wounds do: both speak of honor.—Go, find him surgeons.
[Exit Captain, attended.]
[Enter Ross and Angus.]
MALCOLM. The worthy Thane of Ross.
LENNOX. What urgency shows in his eyes! He looks like a man about to tell of strange events.
ROSS. God save the King!
DUNCAN. Where have you come from, worthy thane?

ROSS. From Fife, great King, where the Norwegian banners mock the sky and chill our people with their fanning. The King of Norway himself, with a terrible host, aided by that most disloyal traitor, the Thane of Cawdor, began a grim battle; until Bellona's bridegroom, armored in proof, met him as his equal—point against point, rebel arm against arm—and curbed his reckless spirit. In the end, the victory fell to us.
DUNCAN. Great good fortune!
ROSS. So much so that Sweno, the King of Norway, now begs for terms of peace; nor would we allow burial for his men until he paid ten thousand dollars at Saint Colme's Inch for our common use.
DUNCAN. No longer shall that Thane of Cawdor betray our deepest trust. Go, pronounce his immediate death, and greet Macbeth with his former title.
ROSS. I will see it done.
DUNCAN. What he has lost, noble Macbeth has won.
[Exeunt.]
